from.place: proof, part (<=): the field-theory criterion that a finite nonseparable extension has an inseparable element

title: A finite nonseparable extension has an inseparable element
statement: Let $k$ be a field and let $K/k$ be a finite field extension [def-pc-field-extension]. If $K/k$ is not separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-field-extension], then there is an element $\alpha\in K$ whose minimal polynomial over $k$ is inseparable.

proof.text: Assume every element of $K$ has a separable minimal polynomial over $k$. For any finitely generated intermediate field $k\subseteq K'\subseteq K$, the field $K'$ is a $k$-subspace of the finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $K$, so $K'/k$ is finite and therefore algebraic. Every element of $K'$ is separable over $k$ by the assumption, and the empty family is a transcendence basis of the algebraic extension $K'/k$. Thus $K'/k$ is separably generated by clause (1) of the definition, for every such $K'$, so clause (2) gives that $K/k$ is separable. In particular, the finite extension is separable algebraic, meaning every element has a separable minimal polynomial.

proof.text: If every element of $K$ had a separable minimal polynomial over $k$, step 1 would make $K/k$ separable, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore some $\alpha\in K$ has a minimal polynomial which is not separable, i.e. is inseparable.
